mongodb.title: Two Sum
mongodb.description:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

Return the answer in any order.

starter_code.python:
def twoSum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    pass

hints: Think about using a hash map to store values you've seen so far.
For each number, check if (target - number) already exists in your map.
You can solve this in a single pass through the array.
mongodb.solution: Use a hash map to store each number's index. For each element, check if complement (target - nums[i]) exists in the map.
mongodb.solution_explanation: Time complexity O(n), Space complexity O(n). Iterate once, storing each value?index pair. For each num, if target-num is already in the map, return both indices.

mongodb.title: Valid Parentheses
mongodb.description:
Given a string `s` containing just the characters `'('`, `')'`, `'{'`, `'}'`, `'['` and `']'`, determine if the input string is valid.

An input string is valid if:
1. Open brackets must be closed by the same type of brackets.
2. Open brackets must be closed in the correct order.
3. Every close bracket has a corresponding open bracket of the same type.

examples.explanation: All brackets are properly matched and ordered.
The closing bracket ] does not match the opening bracket (.

hints: A stack is perfect for tracking opening brackets in order.
When you see a closing bracket, check if the top of the stack is its matching opener.
At the end, the stack should be empty if all brackets matched.
mongodb.solution: Use a stack. Push opening brackets. On closing bracket, pop and verify it matches. Return stack.isEmpty() at the end.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(n) space. Each character is pushed/popped at most once. Use a map for bracket pairs to keep code clean.

mysql.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

mongodb.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
mongodb.description:
You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the i-th day.

You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock.

Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price=1), sell on day 5 (price=6). Profit = 6-1 = 5.
Prices only decrease, no profitable transaction is possible.

hints: Track the minimum price seen so far as you iterate.
At each step, compute profit as current price minus the minimum so far.
Keep a running maximum of all computed profits.
mongodb.solution: Track minPrice and maxProfit. For each price, update minPrice if lower, then update maxProfit if (price - minPrice) is greater.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space. Single pass: maintain the lowest buy price seen so far, compute potential profit at each day, track the best.

mongodb.title: Maximum Subarray
mongodb.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the subarray with the largest sum, and return its sum.

A subarray is a contiguous non-empty part of an array.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum = 6.
Only one element, so the answer is 1.

hints: At each position, decide: should we extend the current subarray or start a new one?
Kadane's Algorithm: currentSum = max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]).
Track the global maximum separately from the running sum.
mongodb.solution: Kadane's Algorithm: maintain currentSum and maxSum. At each element, currentSum = max(num, currentSum + num). Update maxSum each step.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space. The key insight is: if currentSum drops below the element itself, it's better to restart the subarray from that element.

mongodb.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
mongodb.description: Given a string `s`, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

examples.explanation: The answer is 'wke' with length 3. Note that 'pwke' is a subsequence, not a substring.

constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces
hints: Use a sliding window with two pointers (left and right).
Use a set or map to track characters in the current window.
When a duplicate is found, advance the left pointer past the previous occurrence.
mongodb.solution: Sliding window with a map storing last seen index of each character. Move left pointer to max(left, lastSeen[char]+1) on duplicate.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(min(m,n)) space where m is charset size. The map lets us jump the left pointer directly instead of crawling.

mongodb.title: 3Sum
mongodb.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets. Return the triplets in any order.

examples.explanation: The distinct triplets that sum to 0 are [-1,-1,2] and [-1,0,1].

constraints: No duplicate triplets in the output
hints: Sort the array first � this enables the two-pointer technique and easy duplicate skipping.
Fix one element, then use two pointers from both ends of the remaining array.
Skip duplicate values for all three pointers to avoid duplicate triplets.
mongodb.solution: Sort array. For each index i, use two pointers left=i+1 and right=end. Move pointers based on sum vs 0. Skip duplicates.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output). Sorting allows two-pointer search. Duplicate skipping is critical for correctness.

mongodb.title: Binary Search
mongodb.description:
Given an array of integers `nums` which is sorted in ascending order, and an integer `target`, write a function to search `target` in `nums`. If `target` exists, then return its index. Otherwise, return `-1`.

You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.

examples.explanation: 2 does not exist in nums so return -1.

constraints: All integers in nums are unique
nums is sorted in ascending order

starter_code.python:
def search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    pass

hints: Maintain low and high pointers representing the current search range.
Compute mid = Math.floor((low + high) / 2) and compare nums[mid] to target.
If nums[mid] < target, search right half; if greater, search left half.
mongodb.solution: Classic binary search: while low <= high, compute mid. If match return mid. Adjust low or high based on comparison.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(log n) time, O(1) space. Each iteration halves the search space. Use integer mid to avoid overflow.

mongodb.title: Merge Intervals
mongodb.description: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

examples.explanation: Intervals [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so merge them into [1,6].

hints: Sort intervals by their start time first.
Iterate and compare the current interval's start with the last merged interval's end.
If they overlap, extend the end of the last merged interval. Otherwise, push a new one.
mongodb.solution: Sort by start. Iterate: if current start <= last merged end, merge by taking max of ends. Otherwise push new interval.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n log n) time due to sorting, O(n) space. Sorting is key � it ensures all potential overlaps are adjacent.

mongodb.title: Climbing Stairs
mongodb.description:
You are climbing a staircase. It takes `n` steps to reach the top.

Each time you can either climb `1` or `2` steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

examples.explanation: There are two ways to climb: (1+1) or (2).

hints: The number of ways to reach step n depends on ways to reach step n-1 and n-2.
This is essentially the Fibonacci sequence.
You can solve it in O(1) space by only keeping track of the last two values.
mongodb.solution: dp[n] = dp[n-1] + dp[n-2]. Base cases dp[1]=1, dp[2]=2. Optimized with two variables.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space. Identical to Fibonacci. At each step, you arrived from either one step below or two steps below.

The word can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same cell may not be used more than once.

examples.explanation: The word ABCCED can be traced through the board.
The same cell B cannot be used twice.

constraints: board and word consist of only lowercase and uppercase English letters

hints: Try DFS/backtracking starting from every cell that matches word[0].
Mark a cell as visited before recursing into neighbors, and unmark it after (backtrack).
Prune early: if current cell doesn't match the current character, return false immediately.
mongodb.solution: For each cell matching word[0], run DFS. Mark visited by temporarily altering the cell. Backtrack after each path.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(m * n * 4^L) time where L is word length. O(L) recursion stack space. Backtracking is key � restore cell state after each DFS call.

mongodb.title: Reverse Linked List
mongodb.description:
Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.

The linked list is represented as an array for input/output purposes.
hints: Use three pointers: prev, curr, next to reverse links one by one.
At each step: save next, point curr.next to prev, advance prev and curr.
Alternatively, use recursion: reverse the rest of the list, then fix the head.
mongodb.solution: Iterative: prev=null, curr=head. Loop: save next, set curr.next=prev, prev=curr, curr=next. Return prev.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space iteratively. O(n) space recursively due to call stack.

Merge the two lists into one sorted list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists.

mongodb.title: Linked List Cycle
mongodb.description:
Given a linked list represented as an array and a `pos` value indicating where the tail connects back to (0-indexed), determine if the linked list has a cycle.

`pos` is -1 if there is no cycle. Return `true` if there is a cycle, `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: Tail connects back to index 1, forming a cycle.

constraints: pos is -1 or a valid index in the linked list

starter_code.python:
def hasCycle(head: list, pos: int) -> bool:

hints: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare: use a slow pointer (1 step) and fast pointer (2 steps).
If there's a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer.
If the fast pointer reaches null, there's no cycle.
mongodb.solution: pos !== -1 means cycle exists. For O(1) space detection: slow/fast pointers. If they meet â†’ cycle.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space with Floyd's algorithm. Fast pointer moves 2x speed; if cycle exists, they must meet.

mongodb.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
mongodb.description:
Given the root of a binary tree (represented as a level-order array where `null` represents missing nodes), return its maximum depth.

The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.
hints: Recursively, depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
Base case: null node has depth 0.
BFS level-order traversal also works â€” count the number of levels.
mongodb.solution: Recursive DFS: return 0 for null, else 1 + max(maxDepth(left), maxDepth(right)).
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(h) space where h is tree height. Worst case O(n) for skewed tree.

mongodb.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
mongodb.description:
Given the root of a binary tree (level-order array), determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).

A valid BST is defined as follows:
- The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly less than the node's key.
- The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly greater than the node's key.
- Both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.

examples.explanation: Node 4 is in right subtree but 3 < 5, invalid.

hints: Don't just compare a node with its direct children â€” you need global min/max bounds.
Pass down (min, max) range to each recursive call.
Left child: max becomes current node value. Right child: min becomes current node value.
mongodb.solution: Recursive with bounds: isValid(node, min=-Inf, max=+Inf). Check min < node.val < max, recurse with updated bounds.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(h) space. Passing bounds avoids the common mistake of only checking parent-child relationship.

mongodb.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
mongodb.description: Given the root of a binary tree (level-order array), return the level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, level by level) as an array of arrays.
hints: Use a queue (BFS). Process one level at a time.
At the start of each level, record the current queue size â€” that's how many nodes are in this level.
Dequeue exactly that many nodes, push their children, collect values into a level array.
mongodb.solution: BFS with queue. Each iteration processes all nodes at current level (snapshot queue size). Push children for next level.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(n) space. Queue holds at most one full level at a time, which is O(n) in worst case (complete tree last level).

mongodb.title: Number of Islands
mongodb.description:
Given an `m x n` 2D binary grid where `'1'` represents land and `'0'` represents water, return the number of islands.

An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
hints: Iterate over every cell. When you find a '1', increment count and flood-fill the island.
DFS/BFS from that cell, marking all connected '1's as visited (set to '0').
This way each island is counted exactly once.
mongodb.solution: For each '1' found, run DFS marking all connected land as '0'. Increment counter per DFS call.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(m*n) time and space. Each cell is visited at most once. Modifying in place avoids extra visited array.

mongodb.title: Course Schedule

There are `numCourses` courses labeled from `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given an array `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [a, b]` indicates that you must take course `b` first before taking course `a`.

Return `true` if you can finish all courses, `false` otherwise (i.e., detect if there's a cycle).

mongodb.solution: Build adjacency list. DFS with visited states. If we encounter a node currently in our DFS stack, cycle detected.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(V+E) time and space. Cycle in directed graph = cannot finish all courses.

mongodb.title: Coin Change
mongodb.description:
You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount` representing a total amount of money.

Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. If that amount of money cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`.

You may assume you have an infinite number of each coin.

starter_code.python:
def coinChange(coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:

hints: Define dp[i] as the minimum coins needed to make amount i.
dp[0] = 0 (base case). For each amount, try all coins.
dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1) for each coin <= i.
mongodb.solution: Bottom-up DP: dp array of size amount+1 initialized to Infinity. dp[0]=0. For each amount, iterate all coins.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(amount * coins.length) time, O(amount) space. Classic unbounded knapsack variant.

mongodb.title: Product of Array Except Self
mongodb.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

The product of any prefix or suffix of `nums` is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and without using the division operation.

examples.explanation: Each element is product of all others.

constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in 32-bit integer
hints: Compute prefix products: prefix[i] = product of all elements before index i.
Compute suffix products: suffix[i] = product of all elements after index i.
answer[i] = prefix[i] * suffix[i]. You can do this with O(1) extra space using a running variable.
mongodb.solution: Two passes: first build prefix products in result array, then multiply by suffix products using a running variable.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (output array doesn't count). Elegant two-pass prefix/suffix multiplication.

mongodb.title: Min Stack
mongodb.description:
Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.

Implement the `MinStack` class:
- `MinStack()` initializes the stack object.
- `push(val)` pushes val onto the stack.
- `pop()` removes the element on the top.
- `top()` gets the top element.
- `getMin()` retrieves the minimum element in the stack.

All operations must be O(1).

Your answer should be a function that takes an array of operations and returns results.
constraints: pop, top, getMin will always be called on non-empty stacks
hints: Use two stacks: one for actual values, one to track minimums.
When pushing, push to min stack if value <= current min.
When popping, if popped value equals min stack top, pop min stack too.
mongodb.solution: Maintain a secondary minStack. Push to minStack when val <= minStack.top(). Pop from both when they match.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(1) all operations, O(n) space. The min stack always has the current minimum at its top.

Check if target falls within the sorted half; if so search there, else search the other half.
mongodb.solution: Binary search: determine sorted half, check if target is in it, redirect search accordingly.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(log n) time, O(1) space. At each step one half is guaranteed sorted, allowing target range check.

mongodb.title: Longest Common Subsequence

Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common subsequence. If there is no common subsequence, return `0`.

A subsequence is a sequence derived by deleting some (or no) characters from a string without changing the relative order of the remaining characters.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters

starter_code.python:
def longestCommonSubsequence(text1: str, text2: str) -> int:

If text1[i] == text2[j]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
Otherwise: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

mongodb.solution_explanation: O(m*n) time and space. Classic DP problem â€” build up solutions for substrings to solve for full strings.

mongodb.title: Trapping Rain Water

mongodb.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree

mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time and space. Preorder traversal naturally captures structure. Null markers allow exact reconstruction.

mongodb.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence

mongodb.title: Find Median from Data Stream
mongodb.description:
Implement the MedianFinder class:
- `addNum(num)` adds a number from the data stream to the data structure.
- `findMedian()` returns the median of all elements so far.

If the number of elements is even, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Input: array of operations `[['addNum',[1]], ['addNum',[2]], ['findMedian',[]]]`. Return results array (null for addNum).
constraints: findMedian will be called at least once
hints: Use two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half.
Always balance so that sizes differ by at most 1. Max-heap may have one extra.
Median = maxHeap.top() if odd size, else average of both tops.
mongodb.solution: Two heaps (max-heap lo, min-heap hi). Balance after each insert. findMedian peeks tops.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(log n) addNum, O(1) findMedian, O(n) space. Two-heap design is optimal for streaming median.

mongodb.title: Permutations
mongodb.description: Given an array `nums` of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.
constraints: All integers in nums are unique
hints: Use backtracking: at each step, pick an unused element and recurse.
Use a boolean visited array or swap elements to track which are used.
Base case: when current permutation length equals nums.length, add to result.
mongodb.solution: Backtracking: swap nums[i] with nums[start], recurse for start+1, swap back (restore).
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n! * n) time and space. n! permutations each of length n. Swap-based avoids extra visited array.

mongodb.title: Jump Game
mongodb.description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. You are initially positioned at the first index, and each element represents your maximum jump length from that position.

Return `true` if you can reach the last index, or `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 from index 0, then 3 from index 1 to last.

hints: Track the furthest index you can reach so far.
If at any point your current index exceeds maxReach, you're stuck.
Update maxReach = max(maxReach, i + nums[i]) at each step.
mongodb.solution: Greedy: track maxReach. For each i <= maxReach, update maxReach = max(maxReach, i+nums[i]). Return maxReach >= n-1.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space. Greedy works because we always want to extend reach as far as possible.

mongodb.title: Subsets
mongodb.description:
Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set).

The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the solution in any order.
constraints: All numbers in nums are unique
hints: Backtracking: at each index, decide to include or exclude the element.
Add the current subset to result at every recursive call (not just leaf nodes).
Bit manipulation: for n elements, iterate 0 to 2^n-1, each bit determines inclusion.
mongodb.solution: Backtracking: start with empty subset, at each step add current and recurse including/excluding next elements.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(2^n * n) time, O(2^n * n) space. 2^n subsets, each up to length n to copy.

mongodb.title: Decode Ways
mongodb.description:
A message containing letters from A-Z can be encoded as numbers: 'A'â†’1, 'B'â†’2, ..., 'Z'â†’26.

Given a string `s` containing only digits, return the number of ways to decode it.

The test cases are generated so that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: dp[i] = number of ways to decode s[0..i-1].
Single digit: dp[i] += dp[i-1] if s[i-1] != '0'.
Two digits: dp[i] += dp[i-2] if s[i-2..i-1] is between 10 and 26.
mongodb.solution: DP: dp[0]=1, dp[1]= s[0]!='0' ? 1:0. For each i, add dp[i-1] if valid single, dp[i-2] if valid double.
mongodb.solution_explanation: O(n) time, O(1) space (only need last two values). Handle leading zeros carefully.
